links.why: Roti starts as wheat grain that was grown in a field, ground into flour, and then rolled by you.
When you add water to the flour and knead, it turns into a soft dough instead of staying dry powder.
You roll the dough ball out flat into a circle, and a ball and a circle are different shapes.
The tawa heats the roti, and the heat makes the dough puff up and turn brown.
If amma makes 8 rotis for 4 people, each person gets 2, and that is sharing equally.
The heat from the flame makes the water bubble, and the hard dal turns soft.
Dal has protein, which helps your body grow and mend itself.
Dal is the seed of a plant, and the seed holds food for a baby plant.
We measure how much water goes with one cup of dal, and that is capacity.
The gas flame needs air to burn, which is why we keep the burner clear and never leave it alone.
Each grain of rice is a seed, and a seed with water and warmth can sprout.
Rice soaks up water as it cooks, and the starch from the rice makes the water cloudy.
Cooks often use two cups of water for one cup of rice, and that is measuring by volume.
Rice grows in flooded fields, and farmers plant and harvest it before it reaches your plate.
If one cup of rice feeds 2 people, then 3 cups feed 3 times 2, which is 6 people.
The batter rests overnight and slowly rises because tiny living things in it make bubbles.
Not all tiny living things are bad, and the ones in dosa batter are helpful microbes that make it fluffy.
When the batter touches the hot tawa, it sets and turns crisp and golden.
Idli is round and dosa is a big circle, and you can see how a thin flat shape and a thick one are different.
Rice and urad dal are grown by farmers, and they become your breakfast.
The mustard seeds pop in hot oil, and that is heat moving from the pan into the seeds.
Poha is washed and softened in water before cooking, and it soaks up the water.
Poha is made by flattening rice grains, so it is the same rice in a new shape.
You count the spoons of each thing you add, and adding them up tells you the total.
You can write the steps of the recipe in order, with a first, a next and a last.
The steel spoon in the hot chai gets hot too, because heat travels along the metal.
Steam rises from the hot chai, and when it touches a cold lid it turns back into drops of water.
Sugar disappears in the chai because it dissolves into the hot water.
Hot chai cools down slowly, and a thermometer would show the temperature falling.
Wash your hands before you help in the kitchen, so germs from your hands stay out of the food.
Lemon juice tastes sour because it is an acid, and a pinch of baking soda makes it fizz.
Sugar and salt disappear in the water because they dissolve, but the taste stays.
The sugar breaks into pieces too tiny to see, and they spread all through the water.
You measure lemon juice and water in spoons and glasses, and bigger cups hold more.
A lemon is the fruit of a tree, and the fruit holds the seeds.
When baking powder meets the wet batter and heat, it makes tiny bubbles that lift the cake.
The oven heat turns a runny batter into a firm, soft cake.
Recipes use grams of flour and sugar, and a kitchen scale measures weight.
Cutting the cake into 8 equal slices gives each slice one eighth.
The cake bakes for 30 minutes, so we watch the clock and the timer.
Sugar is made of tiny crystals, and in sugar syrup you can see them dissolve and grow back.
Sugar syrup gets thicker as it cooks, and thick liquids flow slowly.
Families make sweets at Diwali, Eid, Christmas and other festivals to share with everyone.
If you make 12 ladoos for 4 neighbours, each gets 3.
The ghee melts in the warm pan, and heat turns a solid into a liquid.
Salt, oil and sun keep germs from growing in pickle, so it stays good for months.
Mango slices are kept in the sun, and the water in them dries up into the air.
Germs need water to grow, so dry salty pickle stops them.
Raw mangoes come only in summer, so people make pickle to enjoy them in other seasons.
Every region of India has its own pickle, such as mango in the south and lemon in the north.
A spoon of old curd has friendly microbes that turn warm milk into new curd overnight.
Curd takes many hours to set, and it sets faster in a warm place.
Curd tastes sour because it is slightly acidic, and lemon juice can split milk into paneer.
Milk, curd and paneer give calcium, which helps your bones and teeth.
Milk comes from cows and buffaloes, and a mother animal makes milk for her calf.
A soaked moong seed wakes up and sprouts, because it has water and warmth.
Try sprouting some seeds in a dark cupboard and some by the window, and compare.
To compare two jars fairly, change only one thing, like water, and keep everything else the same.
Measure how long the little root is each day with a ruler.
Write each day's length in a table and draw a graph to see how fast it grows.
A salad with many colours gives your body many different kinds of goodness.
Carrots are roots, spinach is leaves, and tomatoes are fruits, so a salad has many plant parts.
Cutting an onion into halves and quarters shows fractions.
Cucumber cut across makes circles, and a cut lengthwise makes long strips.
Wash vegetables and your hands before you eat them, to rinse off dirt and germs.
Cut a square sandwich along the diagonal and you get two triangles.
Cutting the sandwich into halves and quarters gives equal parts.
A sandwich with bread, vegetables and cheese gives energy, goodness and protein together.
Bread is soft and toast is crisp, so heat changes how a material feels.
Layering bread, chutney, tomato and cucumber in order makes a pattern.
Hot oil is much hotter than boiling water, so only a grown-up should do the frying.
The water inside the batter turns to steam in hot oil, and that is why puris puff up.
A puri puffs because steam and air get trapped inside the dough.
Oil floats on water because it is lighter, and the two do not mix.
Never put water on an oil fire, and a lid on the pan cuts off the air and puts the fire out.
You pay the sabzi wala and take back change, and that is adding and subtracting money.
Vegetables are sold by the kilo, and half a kilo is 500 grams.
A mandi is a market where farmers and sellers meet buyers, and prices change with what is fresh.
Each vegetable you buy was grown in a field, and someone picked it and brought it to the market.
Different vegetables come in different seasons, such as peas in winter and lauki in summer.
Add up the prices of what you buy and check the change you get back.
Guess if the total will be under 500 rupees before the shopkeeper tells you.
Writing a shopping list gives practice in spelling and writing words.
The kirana owner, the farmer and the truck driver all have jobs that bring food to your home.
Look at the date on a packet, because old food can make you ill.
Washing fruit under running water rinses off dirt and germs before you eat.
A fruit holds the seeds of a plant, and a seed can grow into a new tree.
Fruits have vitamins and fibre, which help your body stay healthy and your tummy work well.
An apple cut in four equal pieces gives each of four friends one quarter.
A cut apple turns brown in air, and a few drops of lemon juice slow that down.
A cup, a spoon and a jug each hold a different amount, so we use them to measure liquids.
A kitchen scale tells how heavy flour or sugar is, in grams.
Half a cup and a quarter cup show fractions you can see and pour.
A spring scale measures weight as a pull from gravity, in newtons.
To make a recipe for double the people, multiply every amount by 2.
Count one plate, one glass and one spoon for each person at the table.
If 5 people each need 3 things, that is 5 times 3, or 15 things.
Placing plate, spoon, glass for each seat makes a pattern that repeats.
A table laid neatly looks the same on both sides, and that is symmetry.
Sharing a meal together and helping to set it is a way families work as a team.
Soap pulls grease and germs off the plate so the water can rinse them away.
Turning off the tap while you scrub saves a lot of water.
Steel, glass and plastic dishes are each chosen for a job, such as a steel plate that does not break.
Oil floats in the water as shiny patches, and soap breaks it into tiny bits.
Used water with soap goes to drains, so using less soap keeps water cleaner.
Peels and leftovers can turn into compost, which feeds the soil.
Worms and tiny microbes eat the peels and turn them back into soil.
Compost makes soil rich so that plants can grow well.
Sorting wet and dry waste means less rubbish piles up on land.
Food left out too long turns mouldy, and mould is a sign that it has gone bad.
A cold fridge slows the growth of germs, so food stays fresh for more days.
Heat always moves from warm to cold, so a hot dish left in the fridge slowly cools.
Water drops form on a cold glass because water in the air turns back into liquid.
Mould and bacteria grow on old food and can make you ill.
The fridge uses electricity to keep cold, which is why we shut the door quickly.
In the freezer, the tiny bits of water settle into a fixed shape and make ice.
Ice melts as heat moves into it from warmer things around it.
Small ice cubes melt faster than a big block, so shape and size change how fast it happens.
Kulfi needs about 6 hours in the freezer, so plan ahead with the clock.
To test which melts first, keep the same amount of ice in each place and change only the place.
Heat turns the little water inside each kernel into steam, which pops it open.
Water becomes steam when heated, and steam takes up much more room than water.
A corn kernel is a seed, and if planted instead of popped, it could grow into a corn plant.
The pop you hear is the kernel breaking open and making the air shake.
Guess how many kernels will pop from one spoonful, then count to check.
Boiling water turns into steam, and steam turns back to water drops on a cold lid.
Heat from the stove moves into the pot and then into the water.
An egg can hold a growing chick, and the egg we eat is not fertilised, so no chick grows.
The pot handle gets hot too, because metal carries heat well, so use a cloth.
A boiled egg takes about 10 minutes, so we watch the clock.
A flame needs air, fuel and heat, and without any one of them it goes out.
A cooker whistle comes from steam rushing through a small hole and shaking the air.
Steam inside a closed pressure cooker pushes hard on the lid, and that is air pressure in use.
Heat from the burner moves into the pot and cooks the food.
Keep pot handles turned in and long sleeves away, so the pot cannot be knocked off.
Hard spices break into powder when ground, and a hard stone grinds softer seeds.
A mortar and pestle or sil batta uses your push to crush things much harder.
The mixer grinder is loud because its fast spinning blades shake the air.
Turmeric is a root, cumin is a seed, and pepper is a berry, all grown from plants.
Every region of India has its own masala mix, and the names change with the language.
Kneading is pushing and folding, and the force changes the shape of the dough.
Dough is stretchy and soft, and it changes when you add more water or flour.
Pull the dough and it stretches, and rest it and it springs partly back.
Water joins with flour to make dough, which is not the same as dissolving but shows how a mix changes.
Wheat flour has carbohydrate, which gives your body energy.
Stirring helps sugar dissolve faster, and warm water dissolves it faster still.
Thick batter flows slowly and thin milk flows fast.
Some things mix in water, like salt, and others sink or float, like sand and oil.
Try stirring and not stirring one glass of sugar water to see which dissolves faster.
Stirring is a push in a circle that sets the liquid moving.
Stir salt in water and it vanishes, but it is still there because the water tastes salty.
If you leave salty water in the sun, the water dries up and salt crystals are left.
The water goes up into the air and the salt stays behind.
Count how many spoons of salt a glass of water takes before no more dissolves.
Sea water is salty, so it is not safe to drink.
A rolling pin is a roller, and it turns your push into a smooth flat dough.
Round balls, flat circles and folded half moons show shapes changing.
Fold a gujiya in half and both sides match, and that is symmetry.
A little dry flour on the board stops dough from sticking, because it lowers the grip.
Modak at Ganesh Chaturthi and gujiya at Holi are made by hand for the festival.
Squeezing is a push, and it forces the juice out of the fruit.
Fruits are full of water that came up from the roots of the plant.
Fresh fruit juice gives vitamins, but eating the whole fruit also gives fibre.
Orange and lemon juice taste sour because of the acid in them.
Clear juice lets light through and thick pulpy juice does not.
A good tiffin has something for energy, for growth and for staying healthy.
Steel boxes keep food safe and do not break, so the material fits the job.
Food in a closed box stays fresh for a few hours, but hot weather spoils it faster.
In Mumbai, dabbawalas carry lakhs of tiffins to offices every day.
Find which lunch box fits best in your bag by checking the shapes and sizes.
Every festival has special food, like sevai at Eid, plum cake at Christmas and puran poli at Gudi Padwa.
Many hands cook together, and sharing food builds a community.
To cook for 20 guests, multiply a recipe for 4 people by 5.
The same festival has different food in different states, and the names change with the language.
Each dish can be traced back to plants, animals and farmers.
Food in the kitchen starts as seeds and plants that farmers grow in the field.
Soil gives plants water and minerals, and farmers keep it healthy.
A crop grows from seed to plant, then flower, then fruit, and then new seeds.
A farmer's work covers ploughing, sowing, watering and harvesting.
Each crop has its own season, such as wheat in winter and rice in the rains.
Water for drinking should be clean, and boiling or filtering makes it safe.
A matka stays cool because a little water seeps out and dries, taking heat with it.
Your body loses water when you sweat, so you must drink to stay in balance.
Fill only as much water as you need, and the rest need not be thrown away.
Count how many glasses make a litre, which is about 4 glasses.
Eggs, fish and chicken have protein that helps the body grow and repair.
Heat turns a runny egg into a solid one, and it cannot be changed back.
Meat, fish and eggs must be cooked fully and kept cold, because germs grow on them fast.
A fish eats smaller water creatures, and we sit at the end of the chain.
Wash your hands with soap after touching raw egg or meat, so germs do not spread.
Jaggery comes from the juice of sugarcane, which is boiled until it thickens.
The sugar in sugarcane was made by leaves from sunlight, air and water.
Boiling the juice drives off water as steam, and what is left is thick and sweet.
As the juice boils, it gets thicker and flows more slowly.
Farmers grow the cane, and workers press and boil it to make jaggery.

acts.name: Cooking with the family and talking about food

links.why: Cooking with a grandparent passes a recipe from one generation to the next.
Ask your grandmother how she cooks and listen to the steps.
Ask in Hindi or your home language what each ingredient is called, and learn new words.
Some dishes are very old, and a recipe can tell you how people lived long ago.
Write down your family's recipe in your own words, so it is kept safe.
A good question is the start of finding out, and you can test it in the kitchen.
To find an answer, change one thing and keep the rest the same.
Some kitchen changes are quick, like toast browning, and some are slow, like dough rising.
Telling someone your question clearly is a skill that helps you learn.
Food holds stored energy, and your body uses it to run, play and think.
Whole spices crackle in hot oil because heat makes them release their smell and taste.
The smell of tadka reaches your nose before you taste the food, because smell and taste work together.
Cloves are flower buds, cumin is a seed, and curry leaves are leaves, so spices are different plant parts.
In the past, spices from Kerala were traded across the sea, and people travelled far to buy them.
Mustard oil in the east and coconut oil in the south show how places cook differently.
A coconut is the seed of a palm tree, and it holds water and white flesh as food for the baby plant.
A hard hit with force cracks the shell, which shows that force can change shape.
The shell is hard and rough and the inside is soft, so one thing can have different properties.
Coconut is used a lot in coastal India, such as Kerala, Goa and Tamil Nadu.
A coconut split into two halves and then four quarters shows fractions.
Roasting uses heat to dry out food and change its taste and colour.
Heat moves into the papad from the flame by radiation, and also by hot air that rises.
Browning happens fast with high heat and slowly with low heat.
A papad can catch fire if held too close to the flame, so we use tongs.
A raw papad is hard and a roasted one is crisp and light, so heat changes a material's properties.
A knife is a wedge, a simple machine that turns a push into a cut.
A sharp knife needs less push than a blunt one, so it is safer.
Cut away from your fingers, keep the board steady, and ask a grown-up for help with sharp tools.
Cubes, strips and slices are shapes you make when you cut vegetables.
The blade is metal because it is hard and strong, and the handle is wood or plastic so it is comfortable to hold.
